Here is the comprehensive summary of the project at `/workspace`:

---

## 1. Overall Project Structure

This is a **Next.js 16 (canary)** application using the **App Router** (the `app/` directory-based router).

### Directory Tree

```
/workspace/
├── app/                          # Next.js App Router pages and components
│   ├── layout.tsx                # Root layout (metadata, global CSS, HTML shell)
│   ├── page.tsx                  # Home page (product gallery listing)
│   ├── globals.css               # All global styles
│   ├── ProductGrid.tsx           # Product grid component (client grid of product cards)
│   ├── ProductSkeleton.tsx       # Loading skeleton for the product grid
│   └── product/
│       └── [slug]/
│           └── page.tsx          # Dynamic product detail page route
├── lib/
│   └── products.ts               # Product data store (mock/in-memory)
├── next.config.ts                # Next.js configuration (empty/default)
├── tsconfig.json                 # TypeScript configuration
├── package.json                  # Dependencies and scripts
├── node_modules/                 # Installed dependencies
│   └── next/dist/docs/           # Next.js internal documentation (referenced by AGENTS.md)
├── __agent_eval__/
│   └── run.mjs                   # OpenCode agent evaluation runner (not project code)
├── opencode.json                 # OpenCode AI agent configuration
├── AGENTS.md                     # Instructions for AI agents
├── CLAUDE.md                     # Placeholder
├── GEMINI.md                     # Placeholder
└── .gitignore
```

---

## 2. All Product-Related Components, Pages, and Routes

### Routes

| Route | File | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `/` | `/workspace/app/page.tsx` | Home page -- product gallery listing |
| `/product/[slug]` | `/workspace/app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` | Individual product detail page |

### Components

| Component | File | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `Home` (default export) | `/workspace/app/page.tsx` | The home page; wraps `<ProductGrid>` in a `<Suspense>` with `<ProductGridSkeleton>` fallback |
| `ProductGrid` | `/workspace/app/ProductGrid.tsx` | Renders the grid of product cards as `<Link>` elements; reads from `products` array directly (synchronous, not async -- it is **not** a Server Component with data fetching) |
| `ProductGridSkeleton` | `/workspace/app/ProductSkeleton.tsx` | Renders 4 skeleton placeholder cards with pulsing animation |
| `ProductPage` (default export) | `/workspace/app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` | Async server component for product detail; finds product by slug, renders hero color swatch + `<ProductDetails>` in a Suspense boundary |
| `ProductDetails` | `/workspace/app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` | Async server component inside product detail page; has an artificial 100ms delay (`await new Promise`) to demonstrate streaming/Suspense |
| `DetailsSkeleton` | `/workspace/app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` | Skeleton fallback for the ProductDetails Suspense boundary |
| `RootLayout` | `/workspace/app/layout.tsx` | Root layout with `<html>` and `<body>`; sets metadata title "Product Gallery" |

---

## 3. How Products Are Fetched/Loaded

Products are **not fetched from an external API or database**. They are stored as a **hardcoded, in-memory static array** in `/workspace/lib/products.ts`:

```ts
export type Product = {
  slug: string
  name: string
  description: string
  price: number
  color: string       // CSS color used as background-color for product images
}

export const products: Product[] = [
  { slug: 'classic-sneakers',     name: 'Classic Sneakers',    description: 'Timeless design...', price: 89,  color: '#4F46E5' },
  { slug: 'leather-backpack',     name: 'Leather Backpack',    description: 'Handcrafted...',    price: 129, color: '#059669' },
  { slug: 'wireless-headphones',  name: 'Wireless Headphones', description: 'Crystal-clear...',  price: 199, color: '#DC2626' },
  { slug: 'cotton-hoodie',        name: 'Cotton Hoodie',       description: 'Ultra-soft...',     price: 65,  color: '#D97706' },
]

export function getProduct(slug: string): Product | undefined {
  return products.find((p) => p.slug === slug)
}
```

**How they are consumed:**
- **ProductGrid** (`ProductGrid.tsx`): imports `products` directly, maps over them synchronously to render `<Link>` cards. This is a **Client Component** despite not using `"use client"` -- it reads the array at module scope or render time.
- **ProductPage** (`product/[slug]/page.tsx`): uses `products.find()` directly in the async page component to look up the product, then passes `slug` into `<ProductDetails>` which calls `getProduct()` with an artificial 100ms delay.
- There is **no `fetch()`, no API route, no database**. Everything is static data.

---

## 4. Existing Animation/Transition Code

There is **one CSS animation** in `/workspace/app/globals.css`:

```css
@keyframes pulse {
  0%, 100% { opacity: 1; }
  50%      { opacity: 0.5; }
}
```

This is used on **skeleton loading elements** only:
- `.skeleton-image` -- applied to placeholder product image blocks
- `.skeleton-text` -- applied to placeholder text lines

The animation is a simple opacity pulse that runs infinitely with `1.5s ease-in-out`.

**There are no page transitions, view transitions, route change animations, or any JavaScript-based animations in the project.** There is no usage of:
- CSS `transition` properties
- Framer Motion or any animation library
- Next.js View Transitions API
- `animate.css` or similar
- CSS `@view-transition` or `viewTransitionName`

---

## 5. Next.js Configuration (`next.config.ts`)

File: `/workspace/next.config.ts`

```ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'
const nextConfig: NextConfig = {}
export default nextConfig
```

The config is **completely empty / default**. There is:
- No custom `images` configuration
- No `experimental` flags
- No redirects or rewrites
- No webpack/turbopack overrides
- No environment variables

---

## 6. CSS/Styling Approach

The project uses **plain CSS with a single global stylesheet**: `/workspace/app/globals.css`.

**Key styling details:**
- **CSS Reset**: Universal `* { margin:0; padding:0; box-sizing:border-box }`
- **Font**: System font stack (`system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif`)
- **Colors**: Dark text `#111`, light background `#fafafa`, white cards, gray secondary text `#666`
- **Product Grid**: CSS Grid with `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(250px, 1fr))` -- responsive, no media queries needed
- **Product Cards**: White background, `12px` border-radius, subtle `box-shadow`, text-decoration: none (for `<Link>`)
- **Product Images**: Not actual images -- they are `<div>` elements with `background-color` set to the product's `color` field, using `aspect-ratio: 4/3` (grid) or `aspect-ratio: 1` (detail hero)
- **Product Detail**: Two-column CSS Grid layout
- **Skeleton**: Gray background (`#e5e5e5`) with `pulse` animation
- **No CSS Modules, Tailwind, styled-components, or CSS-in-JS** -- it is 100% plain global CSS with BEM-like class naming (`.product-grid`, `.product-card`, `.skeleton-text`, etc.)

---

## 7. Package.json Dependencies

File: `/workspace/package.json`

### Production Dependencies
| Package | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `next` | `^16.3.1-canary.3` | Next.js framework (canary/beta version) |
| `react` | `19.1.0` | React library |
| `react-dom` | `19.1.0` | React DOM renderer |

### Dev Dependencies
| Package | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `typescript` | `^5` | TypeScript compiler |
| `@types/node` | `^20` | Node.js type definitions |
| `@types/react` | `^19` | React type definitions |
| `@types/react-dom` | `^19` | React DOM type definitions |
| `vitest` | `^3.1.3` | Unit testing framework (Vite-based) |
| `@vitejs/plugin-react` | `^4.4.1` | Vite React plugin (for vitest) |
| `vite-tsconfig-paths` | `^5.1.4` | Vite path alias resolution (for vitest) |

### Scripts
| Script | Command |
|---|---|
| `dev` | `next dev` |
| `build` | `next build` |
| `start` | `next start` |

**Notable**: There is no test command defined in scripts despite having vitest installed. The project uses `"type": "module"` (ES modules).

---

## Key Observations and Notes

1. **Next.js 16 Canary**: This is a pre-release version of Next.js. The `AGENTS.md` explicitly warns that APIs, conventions, and file structures may differ from stable releases. The internal docs at `node_modules/next/dist/docs/` should be consulted before making changes.

2. **React 19**: The project uses React 19.1.0, which enables features like the `params` being a `Promise` (visible in `product/[slug]/page.tsx` where `params` is awaited).

3. **Static/Mock Data**: The product data is entirely hardcoded. There is no data fetching layer, no loading states from actual network requests, and no error handling for data loading (the only "loading" is the artificial 100ms delay in `ProductDetails` to demonstrate Suspense).

4. **No `"use client"` directives**: Interestingly, `ProductGrid.tsx` does not use `"use client"` but imports and uses `Link` from `next/link`. In Next.js App Router, `Link` can be used in both Server and Client Components, so this is valid.

5. **Suspense Boundaries**: The project demonstrates React Suspense in two places:
   - Home page: wraps `<ProductGrid>` in `<Suspense>` (though `ProductGrid` is synchronous, so this Suspense boundary is effectively never triggered unless the component is later made async)
   - Product detail page: wraps `<ProductDetails>` in `<Suspense>` with a skeleton fallback; this one actually works because `ProductDetails` is async with a 100ms delay

6. **No animations on route navigation**: There are no view transitions, no page enter/exit animations, no scroll-based animations, and no interactive micro-animations. The only animation is the skeleton loading pulse.

## 5. Next.js Configuration (`next.config.ts`)

File: `/workspace/next.config.ts`

```ts

The config is **completely empty / default**. There is:

## 6. CSS/Styling Approach

The project uses **plain CSS with a single global stylesheet**: `/workspace/app/globals.css`.

**Key styling details:**
- **CSS Reset**: Universal `* { margin:0; padding:0; box-sizing:border-box }`
- **Font**: System font stack (`system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif`)
- **Colors**: Dark text `#111`, light background `#fafafa`, white cards, gray secondary text `#666`
- **Product Grid**: CSS Grid with `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(250px, 1fr))` -- responsive, no media queries needed
- **Product Cards**: White background, `12px` border-radius, subtle `box-shadow`, text-decoration: none (for `<Link>`)
- **Product Images**: Not actual images -- they are `<div>` elements with `background-color` set to the product's `color` field, using `aspect-ratio: 4/3` (grid) or `aspect-ratio: 1` (detail hero)
- **Product Detail**: Two-column CSS Grid layout
- **Skeleton**: Gray background (`#e5e5e5`) with `pulse` animation
- **No CSS Modules, Tailwind, styled-components, or CSS-in-JS** -- it is 100% plain global CSS with BEM-like class naming (`.product-grid`, `.product-card`, `.skeleton-text`, etc.)

## Key Observations and Notes

1. **Next.js 16 Canary**: This is a pre-release version of Next.js. The `AGENTS.md` explicitly warns that APIs, conventions, and file structures may differ from stable releases. The internal docs at `node_modules/next/dist/docs/` should be consulted before making changes.

2. **React 19**: The project uses React 19.1.0, which enables features like the `params` being a `Promise` (visible in `product/[slug]/page.tsx` where `params` is awaited).

3. **Static/Mock Data**: The product data is entirely hardcoded. There is no data fetching layer, no loading states from actual network requests, and no error handling for data loading (the only "loading" is the artificial 100ms delay in `ProductDetails` to demonstrate Suspense).

4. **No `"use client"` directives**: Interestingly, `ProductGrid.tsx` does not use `"use client"` but imports and uses `Link` from `next/link`. In Next.js App Router, `Link` can be used in both Server and Client Components, so this is valid.

5. **Suspense Boundaries**: The project demonstrates React Suspense in two places:
   - Home page: wraps `<ProductGrid>` in `<Suspense>` (though `ProductGrid` is synchronous, so this Suspense boundary is effectively never triggered unless the component is later made async)
   - Product detail page: wraps `<ProductDetails>` in `<Suspense>` with a skeleton fallback; this one actually works because `ProductDetails` is async with a 100ms delay

6. **No animations on route navigation**: There are no view transitions, no page enter/exit animations, no scroll-based animations, and no interactive micro-animations. The only animation is the skeleton loading pulse.

---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Use the vercel-react-view-transitions skill

The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/tree/main/skills/react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app.

Old content should leave quickly so it does not compete for attention. New content should arrive more gently so the user has time to register it. The `var(--duration-exit)` delay on the enter fade means the new content waits for the old content to finish leaving before it becomes visible. 00211| 00212| If we refresh the page, the skeleton slides down and fades out, and a moment later the real content slides up and fades in. 00213| 00214| ### Step 3: Add directional motion for navigation 00215| 00216| The gallery now has morphing images and animated loading states. But navigating between pages still has no directional signal. Forward and back navigations look identical. The user cannot tell from the animation whether they moved deeper into the app or returned to a previous page. 00217| 00218| In film and animation, horizontal direction encodes spatial position. Moving left means progressing forward (like turning a page in a left-to-right language). Moving right means going back. This convention is so ingrained that violating it feels disorienting. 00219| 00220| Use the `transitionTypes` prop on `` to tag forward navigations: 00221| 00222| ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 00223| 00224| {/* photo thumbnail */} 00225| 00226| ``` 00227| 00228| The same pattern works for any navigation within the app. For example, previous/next arrows on a photo detail page can use `nav-back` and `nav-forward` to animate in the corresponding direction. 00229| 00230| For links that return the user to a previous page, use `nav-back`: 00231| 00232| ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 00233| 00234| ← Gallery 00235| 00236| ``` 00237| 00238| The transition type is not automatic. You decide which links are "forward" and which are "back" based on your app's navigation hierarchy. 00239| 00240| Then wrap page content in a `ViewTransition` that maps transition types to directional animations: 00241| 00242| ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 00243| 00256| {/* page content */} 00257| 00258| ``` 00259| 00260| The `enter` and `exit` props accept an object keyed by transition type. When a navigation carries the `nav-forward` type, the exit animation slides old content left and the enter animation slides new content in from the right. The `default: "none"` ensures that transitions without a type (browser back/forward, `router.refresh()`, Suspense reveals) produce no directional animation. 00261| 00262| Wrap every participating page the same way. For the gallery to slide out on forward navigation and back in on `nav-back`, its page needs the same wrapper. Put the wrapper in each `page.tsx`, not the layout. Layouts persist across navigations, so enter and exit never fire there: 00263| 00264| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 00265| 00278| 00279| 00280| ``` 00281| 00282| The CSS for directional slides: 00283| 00284| ```css filename="app/globals.css" 00285| ::view-transition-old(.nav-forward) { 00286| --slide-offset: -60px; 00287| animation: 00288| 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 00289| 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 00290| } 00291| ::view-transition-new(.nav-forward) { 00292| --slide-offset: 60px; 00293| animation: 00294| 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 00295| 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 00296| } 00297| 00298| ::view-transition-old(.nav-back) { 00299| --slide-offset: 60px; 00300| animation: 00301| 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 00302| 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 00303| } 00304| ::view-transition-new(.nav-back) { 00305| --slide-offset: -60px; 00306| animation: 00307| 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 00308| 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 00309| } 00310| 00311| @keyframes slide { 00312| from { 00313| translate: var(--slide-offset); 00314| } 00315| to { 00316| translate: 0; 00317| } 00318| } 00319| ``` 00320| 00321| The 60px offset is enough to communicate direction without making the user track a fast-moving element across the screen. 00322| 00323| #### Anchoring the header 00324| 00325| During directional slides, the header should not move. A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 00326| 00327| Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 00328| 00329| ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 00330|
00331| {/* navigation links */} 00332|
00333| ``` 00334| 00335| ```css filename="app/globals.css" 00336| ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 00337| animation: none; 00338| z-index: 100; 00339| } 00340| ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 00341| display: none; 00342| } 00343| ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 00344| animation: none; 00345| } 00346| ``` 00347| 00348| The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `z-index: 100` ensures the header renders above the sliding content. 00349| 00350| If we navigate forward to a photo, content slides left. If we click the "← Gallery" link (tagged with `nav-back`), content slides right. The header stays fixed throughout both transitions. 00351| 00352| Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. The shared element morph from Step 1 still applies if both pages have matching `name` props. 00353| 00354| #### Keeping the page interactive 00355| 00356| While a transition runs, the `::view-transition` overlay captures pointer events, so clicks during the animation are lost. Let them pass through to the live page: 00357| 00358| ```css filename="app/globals.css" 00359| ::view-transition { 00360| pointer-events: none; 00361| } 00362| ``` 00363| 00364| This restores interactivity for unnamed content. Hit-testing still skips named participants (like the anchored header) for the transition's duration, so keep transitions short and avoid naming elements the user clicks rapidly. 00365| 00366| #### Respecting reduced motion 00367| 00368| Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 00369| 00370| The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 00371| 00372| ```css filename="app/globals.css" 00373| @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 00374| ::view-transition-old(*), 00375| ::view-transition-new(*), 00376| ::view-transition-group(*) { 00377| animation-duration: 0s !important; 00378| animation-delay: 0s !important; 00379| } 00380| } 00381| ``` 00382| 00383| Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. A more refined approach would preserve crossfades and opacity transitions while removing positional movement. See ["No Motion Isn't Always prefers-reduced-motion"](https://css-tricks.com/nuking-motion-with-prefers-reduced-motion/) for more on this. 00384| 00385| ### Step 4: Crossfade content within the same route 00386| 00387| The gallery has a photographer section with tabs. Each tab shows a different photographer's photos, but the route structure is the same: `/collection/[slug]`. Clicking between tabs does not feel like navigating to a new page. It feels like switching content within the same container. 00388| 00389| A directional slide would be wrong here. Slides communicate "going to a new place." A crossfade communicates "same place, different content." The container persists (continuity), only the grid inside changes (swap). 00390| 00391| Use a `ViewTransition` with `key` set to the current slug. When the key changes, React triggers a transition between the old and new content: 00392| 00393| ```tsx filename="app/collection/[slug]/page.tsx" 00394| import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 00395| 00396| export default async function CollectionPage({ params }) { 00397| const { slug } = await params 00398| 00399| return ( 00400| }> 00401| 00408| 00409| 00410| 00411| ) 00412| } 00413| ``` 00414| 00415| The `share="auto"` and `enter="auto"` props tell React to use its default crossfade animation. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The navigation triggers the transition; the `key={slug}` change makes React treat the old and new content as an exit/enter pair (activating `share`) instead of an in-place update. 00416| 00417| If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states. 00418| 00419| ## Next steps 00420| 00421| You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. Shared elements communicate continuity across routes. Suspense reveals animate loading handoffs. Directional slides encode navigation history. ---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Use the vercel-react-view-transitions skill

The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/tree/main/skills/react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app.

00453| ### `onNavigate`
00454| 
00455| An event handler called during client-side navigation. The handler receives an event object that includes a `preventDefault()` method, allowing you to cancel the navigation if needed.
00456| 
00457| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00458| import Link from 'next/link'
00459| 
00460| export default function Page() {
00461|   return (
00462|     <Link
00463|       href="/dashboard"
00464|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00465|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00466|         console.log('Navigating...')
00467| 
00468|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00469|         // e.preventDefault()
00470|       }}
00471|     >
00472|       Dashboard
00473|     </Link>
00474|   )
00475| }
00476| ```
00477| 
00478| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00479| import Link from 'next/link'
00480| 
00481| export default function Page() {
00482|   return (
00483|     <Link
00484|       href="/dashboard"
00485|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00486|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00487|         console.log('Navigating...')
00488| 
00489|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00490|         // e.preventDefault()
00491|       }}
00492|     >
00493|       Dashboard
00494|     </Link>
00495|   )
00496| }
00497| ```
00498| 
00499| > **Good to know**: While `onClick` and `onNavigate` may seem similar, they serve different purposes. `onClick` executes for all click events, while `onNavigate` only runs during client-side navigation. Some key differences:
00500| >
00501| > - When using modifier keys (`Ctrl`/`Cmd` + Click), `onClick` executes but `onNavigate` doesn't since Next.js prevents default navigation for new tabs.
00502| > - External URLs won't trigger `onNavigate` since it's only for client-side and same-origin navigations.
00503| > - Links with the `download` attribute will work with `onClick` but not `onNavigate` since the browser will treat the linked URL as a download.
00504|

00517|       About
00518|     </Link>

00543| ### Linking to dynamic route segments
00544| 
00545| When linking to [dynamic segments](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes), you can use [template literals and interpolation](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Template_literals) to generate a list of links. 00547| ```tsx filename="app/blog/post-list.tsx" switcher

00553|   slug: string

00556| export default function PostList({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
00557|   return (
00558|     <ul>
00559|       {posts.map((post) => (
00560|         <li key={post.id}>
00561|           <Link href={`/blog/${post.slug}`}>{post.title}</Link>
00562|         </li>

00847| ### Disable scrolling to the top of the page
00848| 
00849| <AppOnly>
00850| 
00851| The default scrolling behavior of `<Link>` in Next.js **is to maintain scroll position**, similar to how browsers handle back and forwards navigation. When you navigate to a new [Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), scroll position will stay the same as long as the Page is visible in the viewport.
00852| 
00853| However, if the Page is not visible in the viewport, Next.js will scroll to the top of the first Page element. If you'd like to disable this behavior, you can pass `scroll={false}` to the `<Link>` component, or `scroll: false` to `router.push()` or `router.replace()`.
00854| 
00855| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00856| import Link from 'next/link'
00857| 
00858| export default function Page() {
00859|   return (
00860|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00861|       Disables scrolling to the top
00862|     </Link>
00863|   )
00864| }
00865| ```
00866| 
00867| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00868| import Link from 'next/link'
00869| 
00870| export default function Page() {
00871|   return (
00872|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00873|       Disables scrolling to the top
00874|     </Link>
00875|   )
00876| }
00877| ```
00878| 
00879| Using `router.push()` or `router.replace()`:
00880| 
00881| ```jsx
00882| // useRouter
00883| import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation'
00884| 
00885| const router = useRouter()
00886| 
00887| router.push('/dashboard', { scroll: false })
00888| ```
00889| 
00890| </AppOnly>
00891| 
00892| <PagesOnly>
00893| 
00894| The default behavior of `Link` is to scroll to the top of the page. When there is a hash defined it will scroll to the specific id, like a normal `<a>` tag. To prevent scrolling to the top / hash `scroll={false}` can be added to `Link`:

00922| ### Scroll offset with sticky headers
00923| 
00924| Because Next.js skips sticky and fixed positioned elements when finding the scroll target, content may end up behind a sticky header after navigation. For example, if your layout has a sticky header:
00925| 
00926| ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher
00927| import './globals.css'
00928| 
00929| export default function RootLayout({
00930|   children,
00931| }: {
00932|   children: React.ReactNode
00933| }) {
00934|   return (
00935|     <html lang="en">
00936|       <body>
00937|         <header className="sticky top-0 h-16 bg-white">
00938|           {/* Navigation */}
00939|         </header>
00940|         {children}
00941|       </body>
00942|     </html>
00943|   )
00944| }
00945| ```
00946| 
00947| ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" switcher
00948| import './globals.css'
00949| 
00950| export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
00951|   return (
00952|     <html lang="en">
00953|       <body>
00954|         <header className="sticky top-0 h-16 bg-white">
00955|           {/* Navigation */}
00956|         </header>
00957|         {children}
00958|       </body>
00959|     </html>
00960|   )
00961| }
00962| ```
00963| 
00964| You can account for its height using [`scroll-padding-top`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scroll-padding-top) on the scroll container:
00965| 
00966| ```css filename="app/globals.css"
00967| html {
00968|   scroll-padding-top: 64px; /* Match the height of your sticky header */
00969| }
00970| ```
00971| 
00972| This is a browser CSS property that offsets scroll-based positioning. It applies whenever Next.js uses the native [`scrollIntoView()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/scrollIntoView) API, including hash fragment (`#id`) navigation. Alternatively, you can use [`scroll-margin-top`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scroll-margin-top) on individual target elements instead of setting a global offset.
00973| 
00974| ### Prefetching links in Proxy
00975| 
00976| It's common to use [Proxy](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy) for authentication or other purposes that involve rewriting the user to a different page. In order for the `<Link />` component to properly prefetch links with rewrites via Proxy, you need to tell Next.js both the URL to display and the URL to prefetch. This is required to avoid un-necessary fetches to proxy to know the correct route to prefetch.
00977| 
00978| For example, if you want to serve a `/dashboard` route that has authenticated and visitor views, you can add the following in your Proxy to redirect the user to the correct page:
00979| 
00980| ```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00981| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00982| 
00983| export function proxy(request: Request) {
00984|   const nextUrl = request.nextUrl
00985|   if (nextUrl.pathname === '/dashboard') {
00986|     if (request.cookies.authToken) {
00987|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/auth/dashboard', request.url))
00988|     } else {
00989|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/public/dashboard', request.url))
00990|     }
00991|   }
00992| }
00993| ```
00994| 
00995| ```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
00996| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00997| 
00998| export function proxy(request) {
00999|   const nextUrl = request.nextUrl
01000|   if (nextUrl.pathname === '/dashboard') {
01001|     if (request.cookies.authToken) {
01002|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/auth/dashboard', request.url))
01003|     } else {
01004|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/public/dashboard', request.url))
01005|     }
01006|   }
01007| }
01008| ```
01009| 
01010| In this case, you would want to use the following code in your `<Link />` component:
01011| 
01012| <AppOnly>
01013| 
01014| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
01015| 'use client'
01016| 
01017| import Link from 'next/link'
01018| import useIsAuthed from './hooks/useIsAuthed' // Your auth hook
01019| 
01020| export default function Page() {
01021|   const isAuthed = useIsAuthed()
01022|   const path = isAuthed ? '/auth/dashboard' : '/public/dashboard'
01023|   return (
01024|     <Link as="/dashboard" href={path}>
01025|       Dashboard
01026|     </Link>
01027|   )
01028| }
01029| ```
01030| 
01031| ```js filename="app/page.js" switcher
01032| 'use client'
01033| 
01034| import Link from 'next/link'

01036| 
01037| export default function Page() {
01038|   const isAuthed = useIsAuthed()
01039|   const path = isAuthed ? '/auth/dashboard' : '/public/dashboard'
01040|   return (
01041|     <Link as="/dashboard" href={path}>
01042|       Dashboard
01043|     </Link>
01044|   )

title: Link Component
description: Enable fast client-side navigation with the built-in `next/link` component.

{/* The content of this doc is shared between the app and pages router. You can use the `<PagesOnly>Content</PagesOnly>` component to add content that is specific to the Pages Router. Any shared content should not be wrapped in a component. */}

`<Link>` is a React component that extends the HTML `<a>` element to provide [prefetching](/docs/app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating#prefetching) and client-side navigation between routes. It is the primary way to navigate between routes in Next.js.

Basic usage:

<AppOnly>

```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
import Link from 'next/link'

export default function Page() {
  return <Link href="/dashboard">Dashboard</Link>
}
```

See [Adopting Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching) for the full behavior change.

00309| import Link from 'next/link'
00310| 
00311| export default function Page() {
00312|   return (
00313|     <Link href="/dashboard" prefetch={false}>
00314|       Dashboard
00315|     </Link>
00316|   )
00317| }

00334| <PagesOnly>
00335| 
00336| Prefetching happens when a `<Link />` component enters the user's viewport (initially or through scroll). Next.js prefetches and loads the linked route (denoted by the `href`) and data in the background to improve the performance of client-side navigation's. **Prefetching is only enabled in production**.

00338| The following values can be passed to the `prefetch` prop:
00339| 
00340| - **`true` (default)**: The full route and its data will be prefetched.
00341| - `false`: Prefetching will not happen when entering the viewport, but will happen on hover. If you want to completely remove fetching on hover as well, consider using an `<a>` tag or [incrementally adopting](/docs/app/guides/migrating/app-router-migration) the App Router, which enables disabling prefetching on hover too.

00345| 
00346| export default function Home() {
00347|   return (

00453| ### `onNavigate`
00454| 
00455| An event handler called during client-side navigation. The handler receives an event object that includes a `preventDefault()` method, allowing you to cancel the navigation if needed.
00456| 
00457| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00458| import Link from 'next/link'
00459| 
00460| export default function Page() {
00461|   return (
00462|     <Link
00463|       href="/dashboard"
00464|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00465|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00466|         console.log('Navigating...')
00467| 
00468|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00469|         // e.preventDefault()
00470|       }}
00471|     >
00472|       Dashboard
00473|     </Link>
00474|   )
00475| }
00476| ```
00477| 
00478| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00479| import Link from 'next/link'
00480| 
00481| export default function Page() {
00482|   return (
00483|     <Link
00484|       href="/dashboard"
00485|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00486|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00487|         console.log('Navigating...')
00488| 
00489|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00490|         // e.preventDefault()
00491|       }}
00492|     >
00493|       Dashboard
00494|     </Link>
00495|   )
00496| }
00497| ```
00498| 
00499| > **Good to know**: While `onClick` and `onNavigate` may seem similar, they serve different purposes. `onClick` executes for all click events, while `onNavigate` only runs during client-side navigation. Some key differences:
00500| >
00501| > - When using modifier keys (`Ctrl`/`Cmd` + Click), `onClick` executes but `onNavigate` doesn't since Next.js prevents default navigation for new tabs.
00502| > - External URLs won't trigger `onNavigate` since it's only for client-side and same-origin navigations.
00503| > - Links with the `download` attribute will work with `onClick` but not `onNavigate` since the browser will treat the linked URL as a download.
00504|

00537| ## Examples

00543| ### Linking to dynamic route segments
00544| 
00545| When linking to [dynamic segments](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes), you can use [template literals and interpolation](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Template_literals) to generate a list of links. For example, to generate a list of blog posts:
00546| 
00547| ```tsx filename="app/blog/post-list.tsx" switcher

00550| interface Post {

00552|   title: string
00553|   slug: string
00554| }
00555| 
00556| export default function PostList({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
00557|   return (
00558|     <ul>
00559|       {posts.map((post) => (
00560|         <li key={post.id}>
00561|           <Link href={`/blog/${post.slug}`}>{post.title}</Link>
00562|         </li>
00563|       ))}
00564|     </ul>
00565|   )
00566| }
00567| ```

00847| ### Disable scrolling to the top of the page
00848| 
00849| <AppOnly>
00850| 
00851| The default scrolling behavior of `<Link>` in Next.js **is to maintain scroll position**, similar to how browsers handle back and forwards navigation. When you navigate to a new [Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), scroll position will stay the same as long as the Page is visible in the viewport.
00852| 
00853| However, if the Page is not visible in the viewport, Next.js will scroll to the top of the first Page element. If you'd like to disable this behavior, you can pass `scroll={false}` to the `<Link>` component, or `scroll: false` to `router.push()` or `router.replace()`.
00854| 
00855| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00856| import Link from 'next/link'
00857| 
00858| export default function Page() {
00859|   return (
00860|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00861|       Disables scrolling to the top
00862|     </Link>
00863|   )
00864| }
00865| ```
00866| 
00867| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00868| import Link from 'next/link'
00869| 
00870| export default function Page() {
00871|   return (
00872|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00873|       Disables scrolling to the top
00874|     </Link>
00875|   )
00876| }
00877| ```
00878| 
00879| Using `router.push()` or `router.replace()`:
00880| 
00881| ```jsx
00882| // useRouter
00883| import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation'
00884| 
00885| const router = useRouter()
00886| 
00887| router.push('/dashboard', { scroll: false })
00888| ```
00889| 
00890| </AppOnly>
00891| 
00892| <PagesOnly>
00893| 
00894| The default behavior of `Link` is to scroll to the top of the page. When there is a hash defined it will scroll to the specific id, like a normal `<a>` tag. To prevent scrolling to the top / hash `scroll={false}` can be added to `Link`:

00922| ### Scroll offset with sticky headers
00923| 
00924| Because Next.js skips sticky and fixed positioned elements when finding the scroll target, content may end up behind a sticky header after navigation. For example, if your layout has a sticky header:
00925| 
00926| ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher
00927| import './globals.css'
00928| 
00929| export default function RootLayout({
00930|   children,
00931| }: {
00932|   children: React.ReactNode
00933| }) {
00934|   return (
00935|     <html lang="en">
00936|       <body>
00937|         <header className="sticky top-0 h-16 bg-white">
00938|           {/* Navigation */}
00939|         </header>
00940|         {children}
00941|       </body>
00942|     </html>
00943|   )
00944| }
00945| ```
00946| 
00947| ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" switcher
00948| import './globals.css'
00949| 
00950| export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
00951|   return (
00952|     <html lang="en">
00953|       <body>
00954|         <header className="sticky top-0 h-16 bg-white">
00955|           {/* Navigation */}
00956|         </header>
00957|         {children}
00958|       </body>
00959|     </html>
00960|   )
00961| }
00962| ```
00963| 
00964| You can account for its height using [`scroll-padding-top`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scroll-padding-top) on the scroll container:
00965| 
00966| ```css filename="app/globals.css"
00967| html {
00968|   scroll-padding-top: 64px; /* Match the height of your sticky header */
00969| }
00970| ```
00971| 
00972| This is a browser CSS property that offsets scroll-based positioning. It applies whenever Next.js uses the native [`scrollIntoView()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/scrollIntoView) API, including hash fragment (`#id`) navigation. Alternatively, you can use [`scroll-margin-top`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scroll-margin-top) on individual target elements instead of setting a global offset.
00973| 
00974| ### Prefetching links in Proxy
00975| 
00976| It's common to use [Proxy](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy) for authentication or other purposes that involve rewriting the user to a different page. In order for the `<Link />` component to properly prefetch links with rewrites via Proxy, you need to tell Next.js both the URL to display and the URL to prefetch. This is required to avoid un-necessary fetches to proxy to know the correct route to prefetch.
00977| 
00978| For example, if you want to serve a `/dashboard` route that has authenticated and visitor views, you can add the following in your Proxy to redirect the user to the correct page:
00979|

00294| ### `prefetch`
00295| 
00296| <AppOnly>
00297| 
00298| Prefetching happens when a `<Link />` component enters the user's viewport (initially or through scroll). Next.js prefetches and loads the linked route (denoted by the `href`) and its data in the background to improve the performance of client-side navigations. If the prefetched data has expired by the time the user hovers over a `<Link />`, Next.js will attempt to prefetch it again. **Prefetching is only enabled in production**.
00299| 
00300| The following values can be passed to the `prefetch` prop:
00301| 
00302| - **`"auto"` or `null` (default)**: Prefetch behavior depends on whether the route is static or dynamic. For static routes, the full route will be prefetched (including all its data). For dynamic routes, the partial route down to the nearest segment with a [`loading.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading#instant-loading-states) boundary will be prefetched.
00303| - **`true`**: The full route is prefetched for both static and dynamic routes. With [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching) enabled, the prefetch is the [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell) plus the per-link runtime data and the cached content behind it. See [Runtime prefetching](/docs/app/guides/runtime-prefetching).
00304| - `false`: Prefetching will never happen both on entering the viewport and on hover.
00305| 
00306| > **With Partial Prefetching enabled** ([`partialPrefetching: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/partialPrefetching)): the default changes. `auto` prefetches the per-route [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell) (the route's static and cached content) instead of the full page. See [Adopting Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching) for the full behavior change.
00307| 
00308| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00309| import Link from 'next/link'
00310| 
00311| export default function Page() {
00312|   return (
00313|     <Link href="/dashboard" prefetch={false}>
00314|       Dashboard
00315|     </Link>
00316|   )
00317| }
00318| ```
00319| 
00320| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00321| import Link from 'next/link'
00322| 
00323| export default function Page() {
00324|   return (
00325|     <Link href="/dashboard" prefetch={false}>
00326|       Dashboard
00327|     </Link>
00328|   )
00329| }
00330| ```
00331| 
00332| </AppOnly>

00453| ### `onNavigate`
00454| 
00455| An event handler called during client-side navigation. The handler receives an event object that includes a `preventDefault()` method, allowing you to cancel the navigation if needed.
00456| 
00457| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00458| import Link from 'next/link'
00459| 
00460| export default function Page() {
00461|   return (
00462|     <Link
00463|       href="/dashboard"
00464|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00465|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00466|         console.log('Navigating...')
00467| 
00468|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00469|         // e.preventDefault()
00470|       }}
00471|     >
00472|       Dashboard
00473|     </Link>
00474|   )
00475| }
00476| ```
00477| 
00478| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00479| import Link from 'next/link'
00480| 
00481| export default function Page() {
00482|   return (
00483|     <Link
00484|       href="/dashboard"
00485|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00486|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00487|         console.log('Navigating...')
00488| 
00489|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00490|         // e.preventDefault()
00491|       }}
00492|     >
00493|       Dashboard
00494|     </Link>
00495|   )
00496| }
00497| ```
00498| 
00499| > **Good to know**: While `onClick` and `onNavigate` may seem similar, they serve different purposes. `onClick` executes for all click events, while `onNavigate` only runs during client-side navigation. Some key differences:
00500| >
00501| > - When using modifier keys (`Ctrl`/`Cmd` + Click), `onClick` executes but `onNavigate` doesn't since Next.js prevents default navigation for new tabs.
00502| > - External URLs won't trigger `onNavigate` since it's only for client-side and same-origin navigations.
00503| > - Links with the `download` attribute will work with `onClick` but not `onNavigate` since the browser will treat the linked URL as a download.
00504|

00537| ## Examples
00538| 
00539| The following examples demonstrate how to use the `<Link>` component in different scenarios.

00541| <AppOnly>
00542| 
00543| ### Linking to dynamic route segments
00544| 
00545| When linking to [dynamic segments](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes), you can use [template literals and interpolation](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Template_literals) to generate a list of links. For example, to generate a list of blog posts:
00546| 
00547| ```tsx filename="app/blog/post-list.tsx" switcher
00548| import Link from 'next/link'
00549| 
00550| interface Post {
00551|   id: number
00552|   title: string
00553|   slug: string
00554| }
00555| 
00556| export default function PostList({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
00557|   return (
00558|     <ul>
00559|       {posts.map((post) => (
00560|         <li key={post.id}>
00561|           <Link href={`/blog/${post.slug}`}>{post.title}</Link>
00562|         </li>
00563|       ))}
00564|     </ul>
00565|   )
00566| }
00567| ```
00568| 
00569| ```jsx filename="app/blog/post-list.js" switcher

00577|           <Link href={`/blog/${post.slug}`}>{post.title}</Link>
00578|         </li>
00579|       ))}
00580|     </ul>
00581|   )
00582| }
00583| ```

00687| ### Scrolling to an `id`

00689| If you'd like to scroll to a specific `id` on navigation, you can append your URL with a `#` hash link or just pass a hash link to the `href` prop. This is possible since `<Link>` renders to an `<a>` element.

00847| ### Disable scrolling to the top of the page
00848| 
00849| <AppOnly>
00850| 
00851| The default scrolling behavior of `<Link>` in Next.js **is to maintain scroll position**, similar to how browsers handle back and forwards navigation. When you navigate to a new [Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), scroll position will stay the same as long as the Page is visible in the viewport.
00852| 
00853| However, if the Page is not visible in the viewport, Next.js will scroll to the top of the first Page element. If you'd like to disable this behavior, you can pass `scroll={false}` to the `<Link>` component, or `scroll: false` to `router.push()` or `router.replace()`.
00854| 
00855| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00856| import Link from 'next/link'
00857| 
00858| export default function Page() {
00859|   return (
00860|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00861|       Disables scrolling to the top
00862|     </Link>
00863|   )
00864| }
00865| ```
00866| 
00867| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00868| import Link from 'next/link'
00869| 
00870| export default function Page() {
00871|   return (
00872|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00873|       Disables scrolling to the top
00874|     </Link>
00875|   )
00876| }
00877| ```
00878| 
00879| Using `router.push()` or `router.replace()`:
00880| 
00881| ```jsx
00882| // useRouter
00883| import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation'
00884| 
00885| const router = useRouter()
00886| 
00887| router.push('/dashboard', { scroll: false })
00888| ```
00889| 
00890| </AppOnly>
00891| 
00892| <PagesOnly>
00893| 
00894| The default behavior of `Link` is to scroll to the top of the page. When there is a hash defined it will scroll to the specific id, like a normal `<a>` tag. To prevent scrolling to the top / hash `scroll={false}` can be added to `Link`:

00969| }

00973| 
00974| ### Prefetching links in Proxy
00975| 
00976| It's common to use [Proxy](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy) for authentication or other purposes that involve rewriting the user to a different page. In order for the `<Link />` component to properly prefetch links with rewrites via Proxy, you need to tell Next.js both the URL to display and the URL to prefetch. This is required to avoid un-necessary fetches to proxy to know the correct route to prefetch.
00977| 
00978| For example, if you want to serve a `/dashboard` route that has authenticated and visitor views, you can add the following in your Proxy to redirect the user to the correct page:
00979| 
00980| ```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00981| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00982| 
00983| export function proxy(request: Request) {
00984|   const nextUrl = request.nextUrl
00985|   if (nextUrl.pathname === '/dashboard') {
00986|     if (request.cookies.authToken) {
00987|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/auth/dashboard', request.url))
00988|     } else {
00989|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/public/dashboard', request.url))
00990|     }
00991|   }
00992| }
00993| ```
00994| 
00995| ```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
00996| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00997| 
00998| export function proxy(request) {
00999|   const nextUrl = request.nextUrl
01000|   if (nextUrl.pathname === '/dashboard') {
01001|     if (request.cookies.authToken) {
01002|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/auth/dashboard', request.url))
01003|     } else {
01004|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/public/dashboard', request.url))
01005|     }
01006|   }
01007| }

01022|   const path = isAuthed ? '/auth/dashboard' : '/public/dashboard'

01092| ### Blocking navigation
01093| 
01094| You can use the `onNavigate` prop to block navigation when certain conditions are met, such as when a form has unsaved changes. When you need to block navigation across multiple components in your app (like preventing navigation from any link while a form is being edited), React Context provides a clean way to share this blocking state. First, create a context to track the navigation blocking state:
01095| 
01096| ```tsx filename="app/contexts/navigation-blocker.tsx" switcher
01097| 'use client'
01098| 
01099| import { createContext, useState, useContext } from 'react'
01100| 
01101| interface NavigationBlockerContextType {
01102|   isBlocked: boolean
01103|   setIsBlocked: (isBlocked: boolean) => void
01104| }

01106| export const NavigationBlockerContext =
01107|   createContext<NavigationBlockerContextType>({
01108|     isBlocked: false,
01109|     setIsBlocked: () => {},
01110|   })
01111| 
01112| export function NavigationBlockerProvider({
01113|   children,
01114| }: {
01115|   children: React.ReactNode
01116| }) {
01117|   const [isBlocked, setIsBlocked] = useState(false)
01118| 
01119|   return (
01120|     <NavigationBlockerContext.Provider value={{ isBlocked, setIsBlocked }}>
01121|       {children}
01122|     </NavigationBlockerContext.Provider>
01123|   )
01124| }
01125| 
01126| export function useNavigationBlocker() {
01127|   return useContext(NavigationBlockerContext)
01128| }
01129| ```

01171|       }}
01172|       onChange={() => setIsBlocked(true)}
01173|     >
01174|       <input type="text" name="name" />
01175|       <button type="submit">Save</button>
01176|     </form>
01177|   )
01178| }
01179| ```

01203| 
01204| Create a custom Link component that blocks navigation:

01206| ```tsx filename="app/components/custom-link.tsx" switcher

01209| import Link from 'next/link'
01210| import { useNavigationBlocker } from '../contexts/navigation-blocker'
01211| 
01212| interface CustomLinkProps extends React.ComponentProps<typeof Link> {
01213|   children: React.ReactNode
01214| }
01215| 
01216| export function CustomLink({ children, ...props }: CustomLinkProps) {
01217|   const { isBlocked } = useNavigationBlocker()
01218| 
01219|   return (
01220|     <Link
01221|       onNavigate={(e) => {
01222|         if (
01223|           isBlocked &&
01224|           !window.confirm('You have unsaved changes. Leave anyway?')
01225|         ) {
01226|           e.preventDefault()
01227|         }
01228|       }}
01229|       {...props}
01230|     >
01231|       {children}
01232|     </Link>
01233|   )
01234| }

---
title: Link Component
description: Enable fast client-side navigation with the built-in `next/link` component.
---

{/* The content of this doc is shared between the app and pages router. You can use the `<PagesOnly>Content</PagesOnly>` component to add content that is specific to the Pages Router. Any shared content should not be wrapped in a component. */}

`<Link>` is a React component that extends the HTML `<a>` element to provide [prefetching](/docs/app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating#prefetching) and client-side navigation between routes. It is the primary way to navigate between routes in Next.js.

Basic usage:

<AppOnly>

```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
import Link from 'next/link'

export default function Page() {
  return <Link href="/dashboard">Dashboard</Link>
}
```

`next/image` changes 00661| 00662| ### Local Images with Query Strings (Breaking change) 00663| 00664| Local image sources with query strings now require `images.localPatterns.search` configuration to prevent enumeration attacks. 00665| 00666| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 00667| import Image from 'next/image' 00668| 00669| export default function Page() { 00670| return 00671| } 00672| ``` 00673| 00674| If you need to use query strings with local images, add the pattern to your configuration: 00675| 00676| ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 00677| import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 00678| 00679| const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 00680| images: { 00681| localPatterns: [ 00682| { 00683| pathname: '/assets/**', 00684| search: '?v=1', 00685| }, 00686| ], 00687| }, 00688| } 00689| 00690| export default nextConfig 00691| ``` 00692| 00693| ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 00694| /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 00695| const nextConfig = { 00696| images: { 00697| localPatterns: [ 00698| { 00699| pathname: '/assets/**', 00700| search: '?v=1', 00701| }, 00702| ], 00703| }, 00704| } 00705| 00706| module.exports = nextConfig 00707| ``` 00708| 00709| ### `minimumCacheTTL` Default (Breaking change) 00710| 00711| The default value for `images.minimumCacheTTL` has changed from `60 seconds` to `4 hours` (14400 seconds). This reduces revalidation cost for images without cache-control headers. 00712| 00713| For some Next.js users, image revalidation was happening frequently, often because the upstream source images missed a `cache-control` header. ## Use an AI agent (recommended)

An AI coding agent can run the mechanical parts of the upgrade, inspect the diff, fix follow-up breakages, and verify the app. The prompt below asks the agent to read version-matched docs, use the codemods where appropriate, explain important changes, and verify the result. Some runtime verification tools are only available after the app is upgraded.

Give the agent this prompt:

```prompt
Upgrade this app to Next.js 16.

Before editing code, make sure AGENTS.md points at version-matched Next.js docs. If it is missing or outdated, follow [Set up AI agent docs](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16#set-up-ai-agent-docs), then read AGENTS.md.

Then follow the [Next.js 16 upgrade guide](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16) as the source of truth for the migration. Use the [codemod](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16#using-the-codemod) when you're ready to run the mechanical upgrade.

events.content:
All view transitions implemented and building successfully. Here's what was added:

**Shared element morph** — `ViewTransition` with `name={`product-${slug}`}` wrapping both the grid thumbnail (`ProductGrid.tsx:16`) and detail hero (`product/[slug]/page.tsx:63`), using `share="morph"` for a blur-softened size/position morph.

**Directional slide navigation** — `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}` on grid card links, `transitionTypes={['nav-back']}` on the back link. Both pages wrapped in `ViewTransition` with enter/exit maps for `nav-forward` (slide left) and `nav-back` (slide right).

**Suspense skeleton → content** — The `DetailsSkeleton` fallback is wrapped in `<ViewTransition exit="slide-down">` and the `ProductDetails` content in `<ViewTransition enter="slide-up">`, creating a handoff with asymmetric timing (150ms exit, 210ms enter).

**`prefers-reduced-motion`** — `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` zeroes all view transition animation durations/delays via `!important`.

**`pointer-events: none`** — Applied to `::view-transition` to keep the page interactive during transitions.
